text.p: The head of commodities trader Bustan International, Alan Winney, on Tuesday criticised Australia's highly regulated agricultural industry as acting as a barrier to its efforts to become the "supermarkets to Asia".
Winney, the agricultural trader's managing director, estimated the size of the Asian food market at about US$600 billion, about 20 times that of the Australian food market.

"An increasing proportion of this demand is being satisfied by imports, and although Australia is in a prime position to benefit froim this growth, its performance has not been encouraging," he told a commodities conference in Sydney.
The Australian government's "supermarket to Asia" strategy, forms one of the main Asian trade initiatives of the government of Prime Minister John Howard, elected earlier this year.
Under Howard's personal direction, the programme aims to untangle Australian domestic export systems and greatly increase the penetration of Asian markets by Australian food.

Winney told the Asia-Pacific Commodity Markets Conference the cornerstone of the Australian grain market, the Australian Wheat Board's single desk selling system, may have been relevant a half century ago, but was now outdated.

Under the AWB system, grains farmers are free to sell directly into the domestic market but are required to sell through the AWB when exporting. About 80 percent of the grain produced or grown in Australia is exported.
"Risk management or inadequacy of it is one reason why Australia is struggling to fully embrace some of the food export opportunities in Asia," Winnie told the conference.
However, John Campbell, commercial manager for the New South Wales division of the AWB, said the majority of Australian farmers supported single desk selling.
The AWB also offered them opportunities to participate in futures abnd options trading, he said.
"We've gone to great pains to segment our grains-based trading pools," Campbell said. "...It's easy to take a pot shot at the AWB because we've been there so long."
